newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST-Bancomer seen with big 1996 loss.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Bancomer seen with big 1996 loss.

text.p: Grupo Financiero Bancomer may report a big year-end loss on Thursday, but analysts caution that any projections are a shot in the dark after Grupo Financiero Banamex's surprise results reported last week.

Analysts bold enough to predict a 1996 result estimated on average that Bancomer's loss would be one billion pesos, or around 0.16 pesos per share. In 1995, it reported a net profit of 505 million pesos.
"I think they're going to look nasty," said Robert Lacoursiere, bank analyst at Santander Investments in Mexico.

"There's going to be a higher level of provisions in the fourth quarter relative to the previous quarter, because past-due loans have blipped up again as demonstrated by Banamex, and they also have to create provisions in conjunction with the loan sale" to the government's Bank Insurance Fund (Fobaproa) in late December.
He forecast a net loss of 0.20 pesos per share, or around 1.2 billion pesos.

Grupo Financiero Banamex-Accival year-end results stunned analysts because they portrayed three months ahead of schedule its loan portfolio under the U.S. Generally Accepted Accountng Principles (GAAP).
In the process it raised provision coverage to 60 percent, well above the 45 percent required by law under GAAP.

Like Bancomer, at the end of December it sold eight billion pesos of mortgage loans net of reserves to Fobaproa. Without that sale, analysts said, Banamex's past-due loans would have soared far higher than the two times by which they had been expected to jump under GAAP.

Alberto Sanchez of Bear Stearns estimated a per share loss of 0.12 pesos, or some 700 million pesos net, if Bancomer followed the lead of Banamex, it's main rival, and created extraordinary provisions in Q4.
The big question mark in Bancomer's case is whether it will take a similar hit in terms of reserve building.

Sanchez noted that Bancomer has never shown a year-end loss, and its management could find it psychologically hard to do so. He gave it, however, a 60 percent probability of creating extraordinary provisions.
If it chooses not to report a loss, it could do so by using tax credits, he said, in which case it may break even in 1996.

He said another item of particular interest in the report would be the bank's net interest margin, after Banamex showed substantial declines. "I would hope Bancomer will do better (than Banamex) because their deposit base is better. They have a lot of small accounts...which leads to higher spreads."
Several analysts shied away from providing earnings estimates because of the range of alternatives Bancomer has to avoid showing a loss.

Some said it could charge provisions to equity, which would keep them off the income statement. It could also use the full eight years the government has offered as a transition period for banks to create the full 35 percent reserve provisions against their mortgage portfolios required under GAAP.

Prior to GAAP, Bancomer's reserve coverage was higher than Banamex. One Mexican analyst said it may already comfortably comply with the minimum 45 percent reserve requirement and use surplus reserves to cut its losses.
Then again, if it shows a loss in 1996, it is not likely to be a major headache for investors, many of whom have already written off last year as one of disaster for Mexican banks.
